The skills I sought to master were rooted in my knowledge of nature, of tracking, of the hunt. I learned how to manage resources—time, wood, labor—when they were scarce. I saw competence demonstrated not just through solitary skill, but through reliable effort within a community structure.

The detour hasn't derailed my purpose; it has simply broadened the terrain upon which I must prove myself. The goal remains: return home and train the next generation of foresters with true mastery. And if that mastery requires me to be equally proficient in caring for a sick lad’s needs as it does tracking game through deep snow, then this time at the Kettle was not an obstacle. It was merely another lesson filed under *Practical Knowledge*.

The road calls now. I must sharpen my skills again—with bow and knife—but I carry with me more than just experience; I carry a deeper understanding of what it means to be dependable.

My goal remains fixed: return to Highwater and elevate the next generation. To do that, I must become more than competent; I must be exceptional.

The chill of the morning air, though clearer now after the thaw, still carries the deep dampness of the snowmelt. Buttons shifts slightly beneath me, a familiar weight and comfort, his gray coat dusted with dried ice. We are moving again.

When I set out from Highwater, my mind was fixed on forward motion—the relentless drive toward the next town, the next opportunity to sharpen my skills under the eyes of strangers, the accumulation of coin that would eventually buy me not just supplies, but *time*. Time for rest, time for a proper bath, and most importantly, time to build a name worthy of returning home. The road was supposed to be my master, dictating the pace of my ascent toward self-mastery.

But the storm... it changed the map entirely.

For several days, I wasn't traversing the vastness; I was contained by its brute force. Instead of the deliberate hunt and careful travel that defines a ranger’s path, I became a cog in the machinery of the Kettle inn. The meticulous planning—the arrows crafted with precision, the rations measured for efficiency—had to yield to immediate utility: muck, water hauling, serving stew.

It was a forced pause, an unscripted deviation from my grand plan of professional progress. But as I look back on those days, I see the value in that unexpected halt. The road taught me survival; the inn taught me resilience and adaptability. It taught me how to function when every predictable variable—the clear trail, the steady flow of coin—is stripped away by nature's caprice. I learned Angie’s rhythm, the necessity of shared effort, the practicalities of keeping a place running under extreme duress. These are not just domestic skills; they are facets of being a complete ranger, capable of managing unexpected crises with competence and grace.

The coin is light, yes, but the foundation feels stronger now than when I first left Highwater. The storm didn't derail my purpose; it simply broadened my definition of what it means to be ready for the wider world. My goal remains fixed: mastery, service, and eventually, teaching the next generation. But now, I carry with me not just a bow and a knife, but the quiet knowledge that I can survive—and thrive—when the road closes in on all sides.

Overall, it was a practical pause. A necessary stop that allowed me to regroup, earn enough coin to continue my journey without immediate worry, and perhaps gain some unexpected perspective before heading toward Goldwise or further into the grasslands. It helped stabilize my situation; it didn't fundamentally change the course of my training.
